summary.text: Mechanics is the part of physics that studies how force, matter and motion relate to one another among physical objects.
Its basic idea is that forces applied to an object can change its position relative to its surroundings.
Classical mechanics was founded by Galileo, Kepler, Huygens and Newton, and was later challenged by relativistic and quantum mechanics in the 20th century.

items.prompt: An engineer wants to describe how a spacecraft moves along its orbit, and a physicist wants to describe a tiny atomic nucleus. Which tools fit?

items.explain: The spacecraft's orbit and rotation are handled by the relativistic theory of classical mechanics, while an atomic nucleus is described by quantum mechanics.

items.prompt: A physicist models a planet as a single mathematical point, ignoring its inner structure. What kind of body is that model treating it as?

options.label: A rigid body with orientation as an extra freedom
A particle, a body with little known internal structure
An elastic body that can stretch and spring back
A fluid body whose parts can flow past each other

items.explain: Classical mechanics treats particles as mathematical points with little known internal structure; rigid bodies add size, shape and orientation.

items.prompt: Medieval scholars like Ibn Sina and Buridan wrote about a thrown stone staying in motion. What problem were they working on?

options.label: How force on a thrown object keeps it going afterward
How machines can be built from simple gears and levers
How the speed of light relates to the size of atoms
How heat moves from a hot object into a cold one

items.explain: Projectile motion was a central problem, and ideas like impetus and inclination tried to explain why a thrown object continues moving.

items.prompt: Someone says Newton invented every idea behind classical mechanics from nothing. What is the more accurate picture?

options.label: Newton's Principia drew on no earlier thinkers at all
Newton only copied Aristotle and added a few new words
Newton wrote nothing about how falling bodies behave
Newton's work was key, but earlier scholars developed many ideas

items.explain: The Principia is the seminal work, yet ideas on inertia and falling bodies had been developed by earlier scholars such as Huygens and medieval predecessors.

paragraphs.heading: What mechanics studies
paragraphs.text: Mechanics is the part of physics about how force, matter and motion relate among physical objects. Its name comes from an Ancient Greek word meaning of machines. A force pushing on an object can produce a displacement, which is a change in the object's position relative to its surroundings. The word body is used very widely here: it can mean a particle, a projectile, a spacecraft, a star, a machine part or a portion of a fluid.

paragraphs.heading: Kinds of bodies
paragraphs.text: Branches of mechanics also differ in the kind of body they describe. A particle has little known inner structure and is treated in classical mechanics as a mathematical point. A rigid body has a size and shape but stays nearly as simple, adding only a few degrees of freedom such as which way it faces. Other bodies are elastic, which is semi-rigid, or fluid, which is not rigid at all. A spacecraft's orbit and spin are handled by classical mechanics in its relativistic form, while the similar movements of an atomic nucleus need quantum mechanics.

paragraphs.heading: Greek beginnings
paragraphs.text: Ancient Greek philosophers were among the first to suggest that abstract principles rule nature. Their main theory of motion was Aristotle's. A second Greek tradition leaned harder on mathematics to analyse bodies at rest or in motion, perhaps prompted by the Pythagorean Archytas. Archimedes, with works such as On Floating Bodies, and Hero, with his Mechanica, belong to this line.

paragraphs.heading: Medieval ideas about motion
paragraphs.text: In the Middle Ages, thinkers starting with John Philoponus in the 6th century criticised and reworked Aristotle. A central puzzle was the motion of thrown objects. In The Book of Healing (1020), Ibn Sina said the thrower gives the projectile an impetus that lasts until outside forces such as air resistance wear it away. He also argued that, in a vacuum, a thrown object would keep going until something acted on it, in line with Newton's first law. In the 14th century Jean Buridan developed impetus theory, which later grew into the modern ideas of inertia, velocity, acceleration and momentum.

paragraphs.heading: Galileo and Newton
paragraphs.text: Galileo Galilei and Isaac Newton are the two central figures of the early modern age. Galileo's final word on mechanics, especially falling bodies, was his Two New Sciences of 1638. Newton's Principia of 1687 gave a detailed mathematical account using the new tool of calculus, and became the basis of Newtonian mechanics. Even so, many ideas about inertia and falling bodies had come earlier, from Christiaan Huygens and from medieval scholars. Sharing out credit is hard, because the language of science and what counts as proof have both changed over time.

paragraphs.heading: Beyond Newton
paragraphs.text: In the 20th century new discoveries challenged classical mechanics and led to relativistic and quantum mechanics. Einstein's general relativity and quantum mechanics are the two main modern developments, and both drew partly on 19th-century ideas. Modern continuum mechanics, covering topics such as elasticity, plasticity and fluid dynamics, began in the second half of the 20th century.

paragraphs.heading: Mechanics and fields
paragraphs.text: Physics formally treats the theory of fields as a separate subject from mechanics, but in practice the two are closely woven together. Forces on particles are often worked out from electromagnetic or gravitational fields, and particles in turn act as sources of fields. In quantum mechanics the particles are themselves fields, described by the wave function.
